sections.degradationAndStability:

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PB-1 oxidation experiments demonstrate that severe hot-oxygen exposure can generate volatile oxygenated compounds, including aldehydes, acids and water. These laboratory products are not a measured exposure level during ordinary use. For industrial handling, the polyolefin-processing guidance on hot melt, pressurized equipment, ventilation and prevention of prolonged overheating is applicable as family context; the supplied grade’s stabilizers and processing window remain important.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Isotactic PB-1 film oxidation proceeds through hydroperoxide formation and chain scission, with carbonyl-containing material accumulating. The Toyo Soda study identified acetaldehyde, ethanol, water, acetic acid and propionic acid in collected volatiles; it also reported formaldehyde and tentatively assigned methyl ethyl ketone.

Timescales: Product collection used approximately 2 g polymer under flowing oxygen for 7 h at 170 °C, with a 130 °C comparison. Oxygen-uptake experiments used 130–180 °C and showed a film-thickness effect. These accelerated oxidation conditions are not a service-life or environmental-decay clock.

Environmental persistence: Chain scission, oxygen uptake and volatilization do not establish complete mineralization in soil or water. The study does not provide an environmental half-life for PB-1 articles.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: A waste-acrylic-fiber recycling study illustrates a process-specific exposure issue for PAN: alkaline nitrile hydrolysis releases ammonia. Its 160 °C micro-water treatment uses a closed reactor and absorbs the evolved ammonia in an acidic solution. Material and process controls need to include any fiber finishes and mixed-fiber contaminants.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A laboratory route converts waste acrylic-fiber PAN into a useful hydrolyzed polymer rather than regenerating acrylonitrile. In the micro-water study, mixed acrylic waste was hydroplastized with water at 180 °C for 2 h, then ground and screened to isolate PAN-rich powder. A 20 g PAN portion was treated with 10 g NaOH and 12 g water at 160 °C for 1 h, with evolved ammonia absorbed separately. Conversion of nitrile groups to amide/carboxylate groups produced hydrolyzed PAN sodium salt evaluated as a drilling-fluid filtrate reducer. The study does not establish industrial deployment of this particular process or a closed monomer loop.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Thermoplastic-polyimide molding uses high-temperature equipment and molten resin. sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mitsui reports direct mechanical-recycling trials in which injection-molded AURUM was ground and remolded using 100% reprocessed material. These supplier trials demonstrate clean-scrap reprocessing and the importance of reinforcement; they do not establish performance for contaminated post-consumer material.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Parylene-coated devices can be reworked by microabrasion, which creates removed coating and abrasive particles; SCS describes vacuum collection at the operation. Thermal removal and laser ablation introduce different heat and residue considerations, and chemical methods require assessment of the actual solvent. These process exposures are distinct from contact with an intact coating; a coating’s barrier function is not a substitute for controls during its removal.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For parylene-coated electronics, practical reclamation often targets the valuable device: SCS describes microabrasion to remove local coating or expose an entire board for rework, with vacuum collection of coating and abrasive waste. Laser ablation offers precise local removal, while thermal and chemical methods have substrate, residue and solvent limitations. These are commercial repair/rework methods that can enable component reuse; they do not recover parylene monomer or establish a closed polymer-recycling loop.
